title: AI in Education #11: Five Things I Learned from Dylan Wiliam
author: Craig Barton
summary: In the eleventh of his AI-in-education interviews, Craig Barton speaks with Dylan Wiliam, who declines to plant a flag: he agrees both that this AI moment is genuinely different and that education is resistant to revolution, and finds the tension interesting rather than resolvable. Wiliam explains his caution through education's agonisingly long feedback loops (citing Reading Recovery gains that faded years later) and offers a simple personal test for AI use, the difference between offloading (extending your own thinking) and outsourcing (handing the thinking over): ask whether this is something you want to get better at. He is most convinced by AI's proactive role in formative assessment, surfacing likely misconceptions to make a novice teacher more experienced, but warns against collecting more classroom data than can ever become evidence, and against permanently logging children's mistakes. His largest point is that schools may be preparing students for a world reshaped by AI that no longer exists.
points: Wiliam refuses to choose between this time is different and nothing ever changes education, holding both views at once and treating the discomfort as instructive.
His test for any AI use is a single question, is this something I want to get better at, distinguishing cognitive offloading from cognitive outsourcing.
He sees AI's strongest formative-assessment role as proactive, surfacing common misconceptions in advance so a novice teacher can head them off like a more experienced one.
He warns that classrooms already generate far more data than can become evidence and champions decision-driven data collection over data-driven decision-making.
His biggest question is not how AI changes teaching but what we are teaching for, warning schools may be preparing students for a future that no longer exists.
quotes: I’ve stopped saying AI will never be able to do X because I’ve said that so many times and been wrong.
Things that look wonderful in the short term can turn out to lay bad foundations.
Before he uses AI for anything, he asks himself one question: Is this something I want to get better at?
He does not believe in data-driven decision-making. He believes in decision-driven data collection
I think we might be preparing students for the wrong kind of future.
data becomes evidence when it is used in support of a conclusion. Most of what we collect in classrooms is data.
